stories.title: Richard Born Part of Investor Group in BlackRock’s $245M Sale of 600 Third Avenue
stories.excerpt: Hotel investor Richard Born is the unnamed investor in 600 Third Avenue, Commercial Observer has learned. Born joined L&L Infinite, a joint venture formed by former Silverstein Properties CEO Marty Burger and L&L Holding CEO David Levinson, as an investor in the $245 million purchase of the 42-story Midtown East office building from BlackRock, sources familiar with the deal told CO. Born now owns around 25 percent of the property, with each investor owning a roughly equal portion, a source said. Affiliates of Richard Mack’s Mack Real Estate Group, BLDG and BD Blakely were also part of the purchase. Bloomberg first reported the sale, but did not mention Born’s involvement, reporting only that an institutional investor had teamed with L&L Infinite. The deal marks a big transformation for the office building, which BlackRock previously had a 99.5 percent stake in for roughly the past 20 years, with L&L Holding owning just 0.5 percent. Blackrock exited the deal to recycle capital, one source said. L&L Infinite and Born secured a $185 million acquisition loan from Bain Capital at closing to purchase the 1970-built property between East 39th and East 40th streets that was renovated in 2015. Newmark arranged the transaction with a team consisting of Adam Spies, Adam Doneger, Josh King, Marcella Fasulo, Avery Silverstein and Doug Harmon. The property was 93 percent leased at the time of the deal, according to sources. Its anchor tenants include L-3 Communications, which occupies close to 59,000 square feet, along with law firms Polsinelli PC and Aaronson Rappaport Feinstein & Deutsch. Aaronson Rappaport renewed a 42,764-square-foot lease for its headquarters on the entire fifth and sixth floors in February 2025, CO first reported at the time. Polsinelli PC signed a 10-year deal in early 2023, extending its lease through 2036, while also expanding its footprint by 13,129 square feet up to 52,516 square feet. bullets: L&L Infinite, Mack Real Estate, BLDG, BD Blakely bought 600 Third Avenue for $245M
Hotel investor Richard Born owns ~25% of 42-story Midtown East office building

stories.summary: A consortium led by former Silverstein Properties CEO Marty Burger and including hotel investor Richard Born (25%), Mack Real Estate Group, BLDG, and BD Blakely purchased the 42-story office tower at 600 Third Avenue in Midtown East from BlackRock for $245 million. BlackRock had held a 99.5% stake for roughly 20 years. The deal signals a major transformation for the property and reflects ongoing distress in Manhattan's office market.
stories.impact: Office-to-residential conversion attempts in Manhattan (like the failed plan for 475 17th in Denver) are increasingly replaced by strategic repositioning by value-add players. This Midtown East transaction will likely trigger a wave of adaptive-use feasibility studies across Manhattan's Class A stock, signaling potential ground-floor or mid-rise residential conversion opportunities where office fundamentals remain challenged. Watch for conversion equity plays in submarkets with strong residential demand.

stories.title: Office Tenants Should Negotiate Cell Coverage Like a Lease Issue
stories.excerpt: For most of the past two decades, connectivity in office buildings followed a simple division of labor. Tenants bought their own wi-fi. Wireless carriers delivered the cellular signal, and often funded the in-building systems that made it work. That arrangement for cellular signal is over, and commercial real estate has been slow to realize it. Carriers have pulled back from funding in-building cellular infrastructure, concentrating their capital on stadiums, airports and the handful of venues where the subscriber math makes sense. For everything else, including many Class A office towers, responsibility for installing and maintaining a distributed antenna system now sits with the building owner. And owners, carrying a cost they never used to carry, are looking to recover it from tenants. Craig Gillespie (left) and Harry Klaff. PHOTOS: Courtesy Airtower Networks; Courtesy Avison Young This is how connectivity became a lease issue. Most leases still treat it as an afterthought, if they address it at all. The consequences land on tenants from two directions. A tenant can sign for space where coverage is poor and then discover — after the buildout and the announcement to employees — that fixing it is a capital project with no clear owner. Or a tenant can sign a lease with broad operating-expense language and watch a substantial distributed antenna system (DAS) installation pass through as a cost it never expected. Neither outcome is necessary. Both are avoidable in diligence. Tenants and brokers should treat connectivity as a building system, the way they already treat HVAC or elevators: something that needs to be inspected, documented and warranted. Start with what exists. Ask the owner for current coverage test data, carrier by carrier, with the measurement method disclosed. “We have good service” is not data. bullets: Wireless carriers retreating from in-building cellular infrastructure funding
Building owners now responsible for distributed antenna system capex; passing costs to tenants
Connectivity becoming material lease negotiation issue; most leases silent on coverage responsibility
stories.summary: Wireless carriers have stopped funding in-building cellular infrastructure, shifting responsibility and capital burden to commercial property owners. Carriers now concentrate spending only on high-traffic venues (stadiums, airports); office buildings must install and maintain distributed antenna systems at owner expense. Owners are recovering these costs from tenants, making connectivity a new lease negotiation point that most Class A office leases fail to address.
stories.impact: For multifamily developers: this shift creates an unanticipated operating cost and lease friction in mixed-use projects. A residential community adjacent to a Class A office tower may also face pressure to fund its own cellular infrastructure. More importantly, it signals eroding landlord-carrier alignment and rising tenant expectations for connectivity as a baseline amenity—a cost baseline that should be factored into multifamily pro formas, especially in tech-heavy markets like Austin, Denver, and Seattle.

stories.title: Stream Realty Partners Facilitates $25M Industrial Deal in Virginia
stories.excerpt: Stream Realty Partners has facilitated the $25 million sale of 10904 Carolina Drive, a 102,500-square-foot industrial property in Manassas, Virginia. Stream’s Caulley Deringer, Executive Vice President Steve Cloud, and Vice President Andrew Hassett oversaw the sale. The firm will also manage leasing for the property on behalf of the new ownership. Located in the Interstate 66/Manassas industrial submarket of Prince William County, 10904 Carolina Drive features 27-foot clear heights, eight loading docks, two drive-in doors, one ramped drive-in, an on-site truck scale, and more than two acres of outdoor storage. The property is strategically positioned near Interstate 66 with convenient connectivity to Interstate 95, Manassas Regional Airport, and Washington Dulles International Airport, providing access to key transportation corridors serving Northern Virginia and the broader Washington, D.C., region. “This sale reflects the continued strength of the industrial market in Northern Virginia, particularly in western Prince William County, where investors remain highly active in pursuing industrial assets,” said Caulley Deringer, Managing Director at Stream. The post Stream Realty Partners Facilitates $25M Industrial Deal in Virginia appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Stream Realty facilitated $25M sale of 102,500-SF industrial property in Manassas, Virginia

stories.summary: Stream Realty Partners closed a $25 million sale of 10904 Carolina Drive, a 102,500-square-foot industrial asset in Manassas, Virginia's I-66/Prince William County submarket. The fully-loaded facility includes 27-foot clear heights, eight loading docks, and on-site truck scale, with strategic proximity to I-66, I-95, and Washington Dulles. Stream will manage leasing for the new ownership, reflecting strong investor demand in western Prince William industrial.
stories.impact: Northern Virginia's I-66 corridor and western Prince William County are absorbing substantial logistics/last-mile distribution investment tied to Dulles proximity and I-95 connectivity to the Mid-Atlantic. This activity signals accelerating population and e-commerce demand in the DC exurbs. Multifamily developers should track residential supply pipeline and wage growth in Prince William and Loudoun counties—industrial expansion typically precedes sustained in-migration and rental demand in secondary/tertiary rings around major metros.

stories.title: Allied Global Marketing Renews 28K-SF Lease at the Woolworth Building
stories.excerpt: A marketing firm geared toward hospitality and sports is renewing its office space in the Financial District’s iconic Woolworth Building. Allied Global Marketing signed a three-year lease renewal for the 28,098-square-foot office it occupies on the entire 13th floor of the Cammeby’s International-owned building in Lower Manhattan, where it has been since 2016, according to the landlord. Cammeby’s did not disclose the asking rent, but the average office asking rent in Lower Manhattan was $61.34 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “The companies choosing to remain and grow at the Woolworth are looking for more than conventional office space,” Aron Weber, regional director at Cammeby’s, said in a statement. “They value the building’s identity, the quality of its spaces and the opportunity to be part of a community that includes leaders in architecture, fashion, marketing, design and culture. Allied’s renewal reinforces that strategy.” Cammeby’s was represented by David Ofman and Brian Siegel from the Lawrence Group, while David Dusek from Cushman & Wakefield negotiated on behalf of the tenant. “The location was an ideal fit for their employees, offering exceptional access to public transportation,” Dusek said in a statement. “Given the iconic building’s significance, quality ownership and the strength of the location, remaining at the property for the foreseeable future was the clear path forward.” The Lawrence Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Other tenants in the building at 233 Broadway, often referred to as the “Cathedral of Commerce,” include SHoP Architects, which expanded to 56,196 square feet in March, as well as French-inspired restaurant and lounge Goody’s, which took 5,000 square feet on the ground floor in May. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Allied Global Marketing renewed 28,098-SF lease at Woolworth Building Lower Manhattan for 3 years
Average office rent in Lower Manhattan $61.34/SF (Q2 2026); no renewal rate disclosed
Tenant retained despite office weakness; Cammeby's emphasizing community, identity, and cultural appeal
stories.summary: Allied Global Marketing, a hospitality and sports marketing firm, renewed its entire 13th-floor lease (28,098 square feet) at the Cammeby's International-owned Woolworth Building in Lower Manhattan for three years. The average office asking rent in Lower Manhattan was $61.34/SF in Q2 2026, though the specific renewal rate was not disclosed. Cammeby's framed the renewal as validation of the building's brand positioning around architecture, fashion, design, and culture.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, the renewal signals that boutique, creative tenants are willing to accept premium urban office at iconic properties with strong placemaking narratives. This reinforces that mixed-use development anchored by distinctive architecture and cultural programming can stabilize office tenancy. For multifamily operators in Lower Manhattan/Hudson Square, this suggests residential demand remains tied to proximity to these cultural/creative employment nodes, supporting rents despite broader office softness.

stories.title: Seefried, WDP Start Work on 269K-SF Chandler Warehouse Project
stories.excerpt: Seefried Industrial Properties, in partnership with WDP Partners, has broken ground on a new Class A industrial project at 1703 S. Arizona Ave. (State Route 87) in Chandler. Situated on 16.7 acres just north of Germann Road, the two-building project will add 269,100 square feet of modern industrial space to the Chandler Airpark submarket, the city’s fastest-growing employment corridor. Building A will total 69,300 square feet, while Building B will total 199,800 square feet. The project’s Arizona Avenue location provides immediate access to one of the Southeast Valley’s primary north-south arterials, with direct connectivity to Loop 202 via a full-diamond interchange less than one mile away. Leasing and marketing efforts are being led by Dan Calihan, Pat Feeney and Tyler Vowels of CBRE. ARCO is serving as the project’s general contractor. Completion is anticipated in the third quarter of 2027. The post Seefried, WDP Start Work on 269K-SF Chandler Warehouse Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Seefried Industrial and WDP Partners broke ground on 269,100-SF Class A industrial project in Chandler
Two-building project at 1703 S. Arizona Ave., Chandler Airpark submarket; Buildings A & B (69.3K and 199.8K SF)

stories.summary: Seefried Industrial Properties and WDP Partners commenced construction on a 269,100-square-foot Class A industrial project on 16.7 acres in Chandler, Arizona's Airpark submarket. The two-building project (Building A: 69,300 SF; Building B: 199,800 SF) offers immediate Loop 202 connectivity and Arizona Avenue arterial access. CBRE is leading leasing; Chandler Airpark is characterized as the city's fastest-growing employment corridor.
stories.impact: Phoenix metro industrial expansion—especially in Chandler and Southeast Valley—correlates directly with population in-migration and residential demand. Airpark-adjacent corridors like this are emerging logistics hubs for Arizona's e-commerce and manufacturing revival. Multifamily developers should pipeline residential projects in Chandler, Ahwatukee, and South Phoenix; industrial supply growth typically leads wage/job growth and household formation in secondary Phoenix submarkets within 3–5 years.

stories.title: Sephora’s Meatpacking District Store Relocates to 401 West 14th Street
stories.excerpt: Beauty retailer Sephora is taking a walk up the block to 401 West 14th Street. The makeup giant has signed a 4,200-square-foot deal with landlords Taconic Partners and Nuveen Real Estate to relocate its Meatpacking District store one block north from 21-27 Ninth Avenue, according to the landlords. Cushman & Wakefield’s Jason Greenstone represented the landlords, while Virginia Pittarelli of Retail by MONA negotiated the deal on behalf of Sephora. The new storefront is expected to open in the first quarter of 2027. The lease term and asking rent for the ground-floor space were not disclosed, but gross asking rates for Meatpacking District retail averaged $321 per square foot in the second quarter of this year, according to C&W data. The four-story building on the corner of Ninth Avenue is largely leased by a flagship, three-story Apple store. The building sits along an active retail corridor, just two blocks away from Chelsea Market and Google’s East Coast headquarters at 111 Eighth Avenue. Taconic acquired 401 West 14th Street for $34.6 million in 2005, and proceeded to reposition the retail and office building with a renovated façade, new windows and updated HVAC systems. The Meatpacking retail submarket recorded Manhattan’s second-strongest rent growth last quarter behind Third Avenue. While availability has declined, its 17.3 percent rate remains the second-highest in the city after Herald Square. A spokesperson for Retail by MONA declined to comment on the deal, while spokespeople for Sephora and C&W did not respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Sephora relocated Meatpacking District store one block north to 401 West 14th Street, 4,200 SF
New store opens Q1 2027; Meatpacking District retail averaging $321/SF asking rate (Q2 2026)
401 West 14th anchored by flagship Apple store; two blocks from Chelsea Market and Google HQ
stories.summary: Sephora signed a 4,200-square-foot ground-floor lease to relocate its Meatpacking District flagship one block north to 401 West 14th Street from 21–27 Ninth Avenue, opening Q1 2027. Meatpacking District retail was averaging $321/SF in asking rates (Q2 2026). The building is anchored by a three-story Apple flagship and sits steps from Chelsea Market and Google's East Coast headquarters at 111 Eighth Avenue.
stories.impact: Meatpacking District remains a magnet for high-profile retail and tech headquarters, sustaining pedestrian activity and local wage pools. Sephora's relocation signals landlord ability to command premium rents and execute repositioning even in a softer retail environment—a function of proximity to Google, Chelsea Market, and the neighborhood's tourist/cultural draw. This reinforces demand for residential units (especially luxury rental) within walking distance of the Meatpacking/West Village tech/retail corridor; multifamily developers should monitor lease-up velocity in nearby residential buildings as a proxy for local demand elasticity.

stories.title: Harrison Street Adds Three More Former PGIM Employees to Its Payroll
stories.excerpt: Harrison Street Asset Management might officially be on a poaching spree from one particular firm. Two weeks after announcing the addition of three leadership appointments, Harrison Street said Tuesday that it has hired Jon Glass and two others to guide its health care and senior housing asset management operations. Glass, Michael Corsini and Hardie Jackson all join the firm from PGIM Real Estate, the same place from which Harrison Street poached Dan Fanelli, new co-head of its Investor Solutions Group. “The additions of Jon, Michael and Hardie reflect our continued commitment to investing in exceptional talent as we expand our senior housing platform,” Ben Mohns, global head of asset management and real estate at Harrison Street, said in a statement. Glass has spent the last eight years at PGIM leading the asset management strategy for its senior housing portfolio and will continue in a similar capacity at Harrison Street as a managing director alongside Brandon Metzler. Corsini and Jackson will serve as senior associates at Harrison Street. PGIM did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “They bring an exceptional track record of managing institutional-quality senior housing portfolios and will further strengthen our asset management capabilities at a time when the sector is benefiting from compelling demographic tailwinds and growing investor interest,” Mohns added. Senior housing has been a major focus for Harrison Street, which has invested $16 billion and acquired 46,000 units in the asset class throughout its roughly 20-year history. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Harrison Street hired Jon Glass, Michael Corsini, Hardie Jackson from PGIM Real Estate
Glass leads senior housing asset management; Glass spent 8 years at PGIM directing portfolio strategy
Fourth poaching in 2 weeks; indicates PGIM senior housing platform restructuring or talent migration
stories.summary: Harrison Street Asset Management hired Jon Glass (managing director), Michael Corsini, and Hardie Jackson from PGIM Real Estate to oversee health care and senior housing asset management. Glass spent eight years at PGIM leading asset management strategy for its senior housing portfolio. This marks the fourth senior-level poaching from PGIM by Harrison Street in recent weeks, signaling organizational shifts at PGIM.
stories.impact: Talent migration from PGIM to Harrison Street suggests consolidation in the institutional senior housing asset management space. For multifamily developers: this reflects strong demand from institutional capital for seasoned senior housing operators and signals that senior housing platforms remain attractive to large asset managers. Watch Harrison Street's acquisition activity in the next 2–3 quarters; large talent additions often precede capital deployment. Also monitor PGIM's senior housing portfolio for potential distress sales or exits.

stories.title: 16-Story Denver Office Tower to Hit the Auction Block
stories.excerpt: Another Denver office tower is being auctioned off. The current ownership group bought the tower at 475 17th St. in 2015 for $26 million and hoped to convert the office floors to apartments. But that notion fizzled, and now the group, Civicap Partners and Revesco Properties, is selling to the highest bidder. Civicap invests in “attainable” housing projects. The Denver Business Journal reports two other downtown-adjacent properties hit the auction block this year. The 1630 Welton St. building, a 10-story property, is scheduled to go on the auction block beginning Oct. 19. In August, a 149,222-square-foot tower at 216 16th St. sold for $3.6 million after an auction. The 1975 property totals 151,425 square feet. The auction website lists 93,837 square feet available for lease. CBRE is handling it through the auction platform TenX. The post 16-Story Denver Office Tower to Hit the Auction Block appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 475 17th Street Denver office tower hits auction; Civicap Partners and Revesco Properties selling
Ownership bought tower in 2015 for $26M; conversion-to-apartments plan 'fizzled'
Two other Denver downtown office towers also on auction block; 149K-SF property sold for $3.6M in August
stories.summary: The 16-story office tower at 475 17th Street in downtown Denver is being auctioned by ownership group Civicap Partners and Revesco Properties, who purchased it in 2015 for $26 million with hopes to convert to apartments. The conversion plan failed to materialize. This is the third downtown or downtown-adjacent Denver office property hitting auction in 2026; another 149,222-SF tower sold for only $3.6 million in August.
stories.impact: Denver's office-to-residential conversion strategy is collapsing. The repeated failure signals that conversion economics in secondary office markets are broken—likely due to soft rental demand, high conversion costs, or insufficient pre-leasing to justify development risk. This is a critical lesson for multifamily developers eyeing troubled office stock in tier-2 metros: distressed prices do not guarantee conversion viability. Multifamily demand in Denver may be saturating faster than anticipated; hold off on large office-conversion plays and focus instead on rent growth and NOI stability in existing portfolios.

stories.title: Savills: U.S. Manufacturing Jobs, Investment Rebound Sharply
stories.excerpt: U.S. manufacturing job announcements and capital investment are rebounding sharply after months of plateauing earlier in 2026, Savills reported Tuesday. The firm’s latest Manufacturing Pulse cited 78,117 jobs and nearly $70 billion in capital investment announced over the trailing 12 months, for year-over-year increases of 46.6% and 108.3%, respectively. At the same time, the “stall rate” of projects being delayed or canceled reached a two-year low in August. Defense and AI & energy infrastructure continue to drive the bulk of new activity, together accounting for 69% of jobs announced over the past 12 months, with Saronic Technologies’ $3.2-billion Brownsville facility leading a wave of recent announcements that also includes SpaceX, Janicki Industries and Electra.aero, according to Savills. As suggested by the Saronic announcement, Texas has captured more of the latest manufacturing wave than any other state, with 24,615 jobs and nearly $30 billion in capital investment announced over the past year. Pictured: A recently announced SpaceX Terafab facility to be built near College Station, TX. The post Savills: U.S. Manufacturing Jobs, Investment Rebound Sharply appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: U.S. manufacturing job announcements jumped 46.6% YoY to 78,117 jobs; capex +108.3% to $70B
Defense and AI/energy infrastructure drove 69% of 12-month jobs; Saronic, SpaceX, Janicki, Electra leading
Texas captured 24,615 jobs and $30B capex; 'stall rate' fell to 2-year low in August
stories.summary: U.S. manufacturing job announcements and capital investment surged sharply in trailing 12 months: 78,117 jobs (+46.6% YoY) and nearly $70 billion in capex (+108.3% YoY). Defense and AI/energy infrastructure account for 69% of new activity, with Saronic's $3.2 billion Brownsville facility, SpaceX, Janicki Industries, and Electra.aero leading. Texas dominates, capturing 24,615 jobs and ~$30 billion in capex; project stall/cancellation rates hit a two-year low.
stories.impact: Manufacturing rebound—especially in defense, AI, and energy—is a leading indicator of population in-migration and wage growth in industrial hubs (Texas, Southeast, Midwest). Multifamily developers should prioritize site acquisition in metros anchored by manufacturing capex: Brownsville/South Texas, College Station area, North Texas, and Southeast. This wave typically creates a 12–18 month lag before sustained residential demand; start pipeline activities now in Texas tier-2 markets (Lubbock, San Antonio, Corpus Christi) where industrial employment will drive household formation and rental demand.

stories.title: Trademark Secures Financing, to Break Ground on Cypress Retail Center
stories.excerpt: Trademark Property Company and its partner, MetLife Investment Management, secured financing and will soon begin construction on Dunham Pointe, a 202,000 square foot retail and restaurant district in the Houston suburb of Cypress. Trademark will break ground on the 25-acre project on Oct. 1. Dunham Pointe will be anchored by Whole Foods Market, one of 14 tenants that have already committed to the project. Active lease negotiations are underway with more than 12 tenants totaling 65,000 square feet, and letters of intent from more than 10 additional retailers reflect strong demand for the project. The development is part of the larger 1,300-acre Dunham Pointe master-planned community, where strong new-home sales have helped accelerate the community’s evolution from a residential destination into a mixed-use hub for northwest Houston. Dunham Pointe is joining Trademark’s portfolio of Houston-area properties, which includes Market Street – The Woodlands. The post Trademark Secures Financing, to Break Ground on Cypress Retail Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Trademark Property and MetLife Investment Management secured financing for 202K-SF Dunham Pointe retail center
25-acre Cypress (Houston suburb) project; Whole Foods anchor; 14 tenants committed; groundbreak Oct. 1
Part of 1,300-acre master-planned community; strong new-home sales accelerating transition to mixed-use hub
stories.summary: Trademark Property Company and MetLife Investment Management secured financing and will break ground on October 1 for Dunham Pointe, a 202,000-square-foot retail and restaurant district in Cypress, Texas (northwest Houston suburb). Whole Foods anchors the 25-acre project; 14 tenants are committed, with active negotiations covering 12+ additional retailers (65,000 SF) and strong LOI activity. The project is part of a 1,300-acre master-planned community experiencing robust residential sales and mixed-use evolution.
stories.impact: Cypress retail development signals strong residential absorption and household income in northwest Houston exurbs. The success of Dunham Pointe's retail component and master-planned mixed-use integration validates demand for walkable, amenity-rich suburbs. Multifamily developers should prioritize infill sites within the larger Dunham Pointe master-plan and comparable Houston-area mixed-use communities (Woodlands, Katy); these markets are capturing sustained regional population growth and can support Class A rental rents if positioned adjacent to retail/dining/employment anchors.
